title: Abnormal Conditions Break The Interface
excerpt: Abnormal-condition interface failure occurs when a product works under median conditions but degrades under high load, physical stress, exception workflows, or simultaneous faults. The documented examples include petrol retail, maritime HMI, workforce scheduling, space operating picture design, ground control, VHF radio workflows, handheld command-and-control, and maritime traffic monitoring.

bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Abnormal-condition interface failure occurs when a product is designed and tested under median conditions, then degrades when operating conditions depart from that median. The product may appear to work under moderate load, good lighting, trained use, and expected inputs. It may then fail under rush-hour transaction volume, night operation in heavy swell, simultaneous faults, degraded information availability, or exception workflows that fall outside the designed path.

The central issue is not careless implementation. The issue is that the conditions that determine operational usefulness were not made explicit design targets. When abnormal conditions are treated as edge cases rather than core requirements, the failure can feel sudden after deployment while being structurally predictable from the design process.

## Abnormal-condition interface failure is narrower than general real-use failure

Abnormal-condition interface failure is a specific subset of the wider problem where a product works in controlled evaluation but fails in real use. The wider demo-to-real-use gap concerns supervised evaluation, unsupervised everyday use, data mismatch, and cognitive-load mismatch. Abnormal-condition interface failure concerns operational extremes: high load, physical environment stress, simultaneous faults, degraded information states, and exception-heavy workflows.

Abnormal-condition interface failure also differs from general expert-workflow difficulty. Expert-workflow friction can accumulate across ordinary operational use. The abnormal-condition pattern is sharper: the interface may work adequately under normal conditions and then break specifically when the operating state becomes extreme, degraded, or exception-heavy.

## Why abnormal conditions require explicit design input

Abnormal conditions require explicit design input because they are underrepresented in standard usability testing. Representative tasks under controlled conditions often exclude peak load, degraded environments, simultaneous faults, and non-standard transaction paths. These states are difficult to reproduce, but they are not exceptional in deployment.

Abnormal conditions also expose latent interface inadequacies that normal operation can conceal. Ambiguous state communication may be resolvable when a trained user has time to read carefully. Under time pressure, the same ambiguity can become a source of procedural error. An information hierarchy that is only slightly wrong at low load can become dangerous when attention is divided across simultaneous demands.

Exception workflows need first-class interface treatment because they can represent a significant share of operational work in complex systems. Weather events, equipment failure, conflicting assignments, partial completions, and requests outside the standard path may be treated as edge cases in design specifications. In daily operation, these conditions can become recurring sources of friction and workaround behaviour.

## Petrol retail evidence shows peak-load degradation and hidden compensating behaviour

The Swiss petrol station operator engagement documented abnormal-condition failure through 40 hours of field observation across 7 stations, 36 cashiers during live operation, 24 interviews, and a coded corpus of 532 transactions categorised by type and complexity. The peak transaction rate documented was 84 transactions per hour on a single till. Complex combined transactions, including fuel with shop items, voucher redemption, loyalty allocation, and multi-channel authorisation, averaged up to 7 minutes each.

The petrol evidence showed that experienced cashiers had developed personal shortcuts to compensate for field-ordering inconsistencies in the POS flow. These shortcuts reduced friction for experienced staff under normal conditions. Under peak load, they became procedurally entrenched. The efficient path used by experienced cashiers had diverged from the documented path, so new staff could not learn the correct procedure simply by observing experienced colleagues.

The 532-transaction corpus made a hidden pattern visible. Some transaction types were rarely mentioned by cashiers as problems, but were disproportionately represented in error recovery sequences. Cashiers had normalised compensating behaviour to the point where it no longer appeared as a problem in self-report. In this case, the interface did not break visibly. It degraded in a way experienced users had learned to manage, leaving the cost invisible until behaviour was counted.

## Torqeedo maritime evidence shows physical operating conditions as design requirements

The Torqeedo hybrid electric vessel HMI was deployed on professional vessels operating in temperatures from −5°C to +35°C, in rain, in night conditions from late evening through early morning, under vibration, sharp vessel movement, and glare from cold water. In this maritime context, these conditions were normal operating conditions rather than edge cases.

Twelve sea trials over 6 months with 15 professional captains documented how these conditions affected interface performance. The observations included how glare from cold water reduces contrast differently from other light sources, how vibration affects readability at the pixel level, how scanning patterns during night harbour manoeuvres differ from daytime open-water operation, and how information instability under physical stress affects crew performance.

The Torqeedo alarm system, including contrast, visibility, and hierarchy rules, was defined through sea trial testing under vibration, night conditions, and glare. The night mode typography and contrast rules were defined specifically for late-evening through early-morning operations. These findings depended on observing the interface under the conditions that determined its performance.

## Cox Marine evidence shows simultaneous faults and night-vision constraints

Cox Marine cluster displays are deployed on fast patrol craft, racing boats, and workboats. The helm environment at speed includes sustained vibration, hull slamming, and spray. Operators brace with both feet and wear gloves. The interface must remain readable in direct sunlight, heavy overcast, and night conditions including military night vision modes.

Scenario testing during Concept Convergence identified a multi-engine fault issue. Early layouts made fault presence visible, but did not help operators identify which engine required priority attention. When multiple faults were present simultaneously, the operator had to scan each engine state and make a priority assessment under high-speed vessel conditions. The design response was to redesign alarm state highlighting within engine tiles and establish a fixed display area where the highest-priority fault is always summarised.

The Cox Marine work also identified that initial colour choices for the alarm palette interfered with military night vision equipment. The palette and contrast were revised in response to direct scenario testing. Both findings were invisible under normal display and lighting conditions and were found by testing against abnormal conditions the product would face.

## KISPE Space evidence uses a synthetic adversarial fixture, not operational data

For KISPE Space, Creative Navy designed a common space operating picture against a synthetic demonstration scenario that was deliberately adversarial. The fixture was built so that a design working only on the happy path would fail visibly.

At the fixture moment, the imagery feed is down, the newest image will not render, the highest-resolution image covers only part of the area, one image is restricted, the positioning fix is stale while the communications reading is current, and a predicted overflight has not happened yet. Each condition is a designed trap the interface has to avoid.

The KISPE Space scenario is a designed test fixture, not data. It does not represent a real location, operation, satellite, or advisory. The engagement's verification and acceptance material was specified, not executed, so the KISPE Space example should not be described as a completed test.

## Schone Airspace Group evidence uses a separate adversarial fixture for control-channel degradation

In the Schone Airspace Group engagement, Creative Navy worked on a ground control station through which remote pilots command connected aircraft. The demonstration scenario was adversarial on purpose.

At the fixture moment, one aircraft's link is degrading, its telemetry is ageing, a warning belongs to an aircraft that is not under command, the offline map is incomplete while reporting a completed download, and the planning estimate on screen belongs to a superseded revision. Each condition is a trap the interface has to avoid.

The Schone Airspace Group scenario is a designed test fixture, not observations. The aircraft, mission, site, and link failure do not represent a real location, operation, aircraft, or incident. This evidence basis is separate from the KISPE Space fixture and from the handheld command-and-control engagement.

## Raymarine evidence shows degraded states specified during UX development sprints

For Raymarine, on the next generation of its fixed-mount VHF line, the documented precedent is the Ray53, Ray63, and Ray73; the new radio's name is not used. Degraded states were specified inside the three UX development sprints rather than after them.

The sprint covering safety, degradation, and integration specified outgoing distress, received distress, and locally initiated man overboard as three different workflows. It constructed four priority levels with cross-state rules, documented forty-three exception cases with feedback, action constraints, and recovery, and assigned twenty-eight functions to the radio, the chartplotter, or a shared information boundary.

The Raymarine exception catalogue described forty-three exception records across eight independent state axes: voice radio state, display context, calling transaction, AIS data quality, positioning, safety incident, interruption, and chartplotter link. The governing statement was that a current screen is not a system state, and that the interface is a state interpreter rather than the source of truth for radio outcomes.

The Raymarine catalogue was partly evaluated. The interruption, position, receiver, and connectivity cases were put to operators in bench sessions. The other thirty-odd cases were not. Nothing was tested in field conditions: no sea trials, glare, gloves, or vibration.

## Handheld command-and-control evidence treats interference as an expected condition

For a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, including one-way effectors, and the tactical command-and-control software that operates them, Creative Navy authored a system requirement stating that electromagnetic interference should be treated as an expected operating condition rather than an exceptional failure. The reason given was that contested electromagnetic conditions are core to the intended environment.

In the same engagement, signal recovery replaced return-to-home on the first push button at the client's suggestion. Signal recovery was described as a manoeuvre in which the vehicle climbs and loiters in order to reacquire the link, rather than a command to come back.

This handheld command-and-control engagement is distinct from Schone Airspace Group. Schone Airspace Group concerns degradation of the control channel of a desktop ground station. The handheld engagement treats interference as a designed-for operating condition of a handheld controller. Creative Navy designed the surface through which a human supervises the system; it did not design the system, the datalink, the effector, or any autonomous behaviour.

## Maritime traffic monitoring evidence shows freshness and replay failures in audited software

In an engagement for a European vendor of maritime traffic monitoring, inland navigation, and communications software for port authorities, coastal administrations, and waterway operators, Creative Navy's audit of existing software found two abnormal-condition failures.

The first failure concerned freshness. Time of last observation sat behind secondary inspection, so in a degraded state a retained target could keep the same visual treatment as an updating one. The display did not reliably tell the operator whether a marker represented a current observation or a last known position. An equipment view with no state data could also read as an equipment view with no faults.

The second failure concerned replay. The historical view did not maintain a sufficiently prominent, persistent distinction from live operation. Some historical links moved within the recording while others returned towards live, without consistently different cues. Track history could open in a detached panel with weak recovery to the original investigation. Exported views could omit the temporal mode and active layer configuration.

These findings describe the audited client's existing software. They are not general claims about the maritime traffic monitoring sector.

## Triopsis evidence shows exception workflows as daily operational reality

The Triopsis workforce management platform served schedulers planning thousands of weekly interventions for utilities and road maintenance operations. Weather incidents, delayed jobs, partial completions, conflicting equipment availability, and urgent crew reassignments were significant and predictable parts of daily scheduling work.

The legacy interface treated those conditions as edge cases. Exception handling required workarounds, corrective paths were long, and the interface did not provide first-class treatment for conditions that experienced schedulers spent a substantial portion of their day managing.

Three in-situ observation sessions documented schedulers managing peak-load conditions before redesign decisions were made. The observed conditions included simultaneous weather incidents, conflicting job locations, overlapping assignments, and crew shortages occurring concurrently. The redesign treated these as normal workflow states. Weather incidents, partial completions, and delayed jobs received explicit interface treatment. Predictive conflict indicators surfaced problems before users encountered them mid-task.

Productivity was measured in the live product through product analytics: 62% faster job discovery, 83% faster job sequence optimisation, and 58% faster weekly planning. These figures are from real users under real operational conditions. The available evidence frames the gains as partly a function of exception handling being designed for rather than worked around.

## How Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses abnormal conditions

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses abnormal-condition interface failure by making operational extremes explicit design inputs. In the examples on this page, those inputs include physical environment stress, peak-load transaction rates, simultaneous fault states, degraded information availability, and exception workflows.

Domain learning is the practice that documents the full range of operating conditions before design decisions are made. The Torqeedo work required 12 sea trials over 6 months because the performance-determining maritime conditions could not be reproduced another way. The Cox Marine work required understanding NMEA 2000 telemetry behaviour under varying load states because telemetry criticality changes between low-speed and high-speed operation. The petrol work required 40 hours of field observation and a 532-transaction coded corpus because failure patterns were invisible in interview self-report and visible in operational data.

Scenario-based validation uses abnormal conditions as explicit evaluation criteria during Iterative System Building. A layout that passes normal-condition evaluation may fail during a multi-engine fault scenario, a night-conditions test, or a peak-load observation session. Building and testing against these scenarios before deployment is the distinction made on this page between ordinary interface evaluation and performance in reality.

## Evidence boundaries for abnormal-condition interface claims

The evidence bases on this page are intentionally asymmetric. Field observation, sea trials, scenario testing, synthetic fixtures, bench sessions, audits, and live product analytics do not carry the same evidential weight and should not be blended into a single claim.

KISPE Space material was specified against a synthetic fixture and was not executed as a completed test. Schone Airspace Group material concerns a different synthetic fixture for a ground control station. Raymarine's exception catalogue was only partly evaluated in bench sessions, and no Raymarine field conditions were tested.

The handheld command-and-control engagement concerns a handheld controller surface and an interference requirement. It does not support claims about the datalink, effector, autonomous behaviour, safety certification, weapons review, or regulatory status.

The maritime traffic monitoring audit describes failures in one client's existing software. It does not establish a general claim about all maritime traffic monitoring systems.

## Related pages

This situation should be read alongside the page on products that work in demos but not in real use, because abnormal conditions are a specific subset of real-use mismatch. It should also be read alongside the page on expert workflows being hard to operate, because abnormal-condition failure is a sharper case where an interface may work under normal conditions and break under extreme or degraded ones.
